Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we outline general robustness validation strategies for all categories. Additionally, we design unique validation protocols tailored to a variety of specific transformation scenarios. Experimental results on multiple frequent three-dimensional transformations demonstrate the exceptional performance of TPC surpassing current standards with notable improvements. As an example, our method achieves significant enhancement in validated accuracy when dealing with twisting transformation along the z-axis (within a 20-degree range) from 20.3% to 83.8%. All code and models are available for use at https://github.com/Qianhewu/Point-Cloud-Smoothing.

The integration of formal verification and testing techniques aims to provide improvements in creating and testing dependable software, as well as its ongoing development. Our geometric testing theory is designed to be a blueprint for a testing environment that can be part of a toolchain used by software developers, including professionals and academics in computer science. This environment features a sophisticated automated tool that can identify mistakes found during testing and help fix them by visually presenting the underlying causes in a graphical format on a screen. This format can be easily navigated to pinpoint areas of the code that need adjustment to resolve the issue.

We provide a detailed explanation for a part of Serre's conjecture related to GL_2 through Kummer theory, thereby bypassing the reliance on p-adic Hodge theory. This involves utilizing descriptions of crystalline extension reductions, Kummer theory, Abrashkin's findings, local class field theory, Dembele-Diamond-Roberts' earlier work, Brueckner-Shaferevich-Vostokov's reciprocity laws and their implications to describe and calculate certain G_K-Artin-Scheier cocycles.

Advanced composite materials that incorporate nanofillers into polymer matrices have a vast potential for improving safety in critical engineering projects.
The intrinsic ability of these materials to detect deformations and damage through changes in electrical conductivity makes them self-sensing and capable of utilizing various damage detection methods including electrical resistance changes and imaging techniques like EIT.
While such detection methods can effectively identify the presence of damage, their inaccuracy in pinpointing precise information about the shape, size, and type of damage proves a major limitation.
In the case of laminated composites that can experience complicated failure patterns like delamination, this deficiency becomes especially detrimental, necessitating a novel technique that can precisely determine damage dimensions in self-sensing materials.
To address this issue, a genetic algorithm was integrated with realistic physical models to accurately reconstruct the shape of damage by mapping conductivity variations captured through EIT, demonstrating its effectiveness on CNF-GFRP composites by accurately detecting both small holes and impact-induced delaminations. 
The successful results illustrate the capability of coupling piezoresistive properties with imaging and physics-based analysis to enhance the capacity of self-sensing composite materials to accurately determine damage configurations.

Redefining tensor theory for practical applications, particularly in physics, requires incorporating geometric concepts into the mathematics. This paper proposes a comprehensive framework where Euclidean space is defined by two sets of geometric operations: a consistent method for comparing vectors and a way to compute the magnitude of their difference. These operations enable the application of inequality principles, specifically those related to norms, to establish theoretical foundations. Building on this basis, we define and derive fundamental geometric concepts, including the notions of parallelism, orthogonality, and the calculation of angles between vectors. Furthermore, we generalize these definitions to describe the conditions under which a subset of the vector space is considered a subspace.

If a right-angled Artin group acting minimally on a tree that is not a line has a non-trivial action, we prove that its graph $\Gamma$ contains a connected component whose subgroup acts transitively on an edge of the tree.

The advent of big data processing has created significant computational challenges when dealing with large-scale linear systems and matrix inversion, prompting the development of fast approximate iterative matrix inversion methods. Leveraging GPU acceleration, researchers have explored alternatives to classic direct inversion, leading to various methods such as Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and Successive Over-Relaxation. In response, we introduce a new iterative algorithm called 'Nested Neumann' (NN), which builds on the Neumann Series by incorporating a free iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, utilizing an inception depth to enhance convergence. Theoretical analysis has proven that NN meets three key conditions: it converges given the spectral norm condition is satisfied, achieves a convergence rate of one order higher with a inception depth of two, and has its final convergence rate determined by the inception depth. Through a comparison of methods using both synthetic and real-world datasets, we found that Nested Neumann (NN) outperforms existing iterations in terms of accuracy, particularly when using larger preconditioning updates, and the optimization is directly influenced by the initial matrix's properties and the chosen update size.

Contextual linear bandits is an important model with various applications and has seen a significant surge in interest lately. This surge particularly occurred in the realm of wireless applications, where communication constraints pose a significant performance obstacle. Especially in scenarios where context dimensions are substantial. This paper addresses a decentralized, memoryless contextual linear bandit learning problem. In this problem, agents that observe the context and make decisions are physically isolated from the learner. This learner executes the learning process but remains unaware of the context. Contexts are assumed to be generated randomly and a new approach is presented. This approach uses approximately five context dimensions' worth of information when the context distribution is unknown. When the distribution is known, no information about the context is required. This approach achieves nearly optimal regret bounds. Several experiments are conducted to validate these theoretical findings.

A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases, potentially influencing how particles develop and settle within these areas. While the VSI can generate turbulence and, as a result, impact the development and settling of particles, dust depletion might also suppress the VSI, as it limits gas cooling efficiency. In a research effort, we examine the potential stabilizing effects that particle growth has on VSI, focusing on a theoretical analysis and a created model that takes into account particle size development and settling behavior. Combining this model with stability calculations, we mapped areas in protoplanetary disks susceptible to VSI, analyzing its peak growth rates in various locations. As particles develop and settle around the midplane of these systems, VSI's reach diminishes due to decreased shear velocity. In a default model with a 0.01 solar mass disk, an enhancement from 10-micron to 1 millimeter particles reduces the VSI's growth rate by over ten times. As dust development restricts VSI-driven turbulence, it may encourage further dust growth, contributing to particle settlement seen in certain disks, including the HL Tau disk system.

We prove that for two Riemannian manifolds where the Ricci curvature evolves according to a specific geometric flow, the scalar curvature remains constant, thus terminating this geometric transformation. This proof builds upon a previous geometric theorem by Gromov and Li-Yau, adapting it to our particular context.

Recent advancements in outsourcing training and machine learning as a service have created innovative threats such as hidden functionalities that are embedded in artificial neural networks. In typical research scenarios, triggers that activate these embedded features are static in their positioning and pattern, thus enabling detection mechanisms to function effectively. However, researchers have recently discovered methods like Neural Cleanse and AFK, which automate the process of injecting artificial behaviors into networks, akin to political figures corrupting themselves for power. These automated techniques are manual in nature, requiring human involvement in the initial stage, thus limiting their application scope. What's more, injected functionalities found so far are inactive until they reach a certain threshold, resulting in subtle behaviors that go unnoticed. Building upon these findings, we introduce a novel concept called "dynamic backdoors," which utilizes a previously identified mechanism known as convolutional neural network post-processing technique called average global pooling, thus creating a fully automatic injection process that imparts new functionalities onto neural networks. One of the demonstrated applications of this new concept involves a machine learning model designed to detect threats, which was shown to be compromised, resulting in it yielding new predictions for previously unrecognized input images. In contrast to previously injected behaviors, the proposed technique produces a unified activation state across the average pooling layer, thus bypassing detection mechanisms designed to find traditional triggers and enhancing the difficulty level of removing embedded functionalities. What's more, the proposed concept demonstrates high success rates, achieving up to 99.6% efficacy in applications, outperforming existing techniques by

In the context of a parameter serverless federated learning system with async updates, we address issues related to non-i.i.d. data. Our novel 'M3L2' active learning method aims to enhance model accuracy at the end of each learning round. By incorporating a random walk strategy that considers only local data for model updating, we reduce communication needs and save energy, as well as minimize bias during learning rounds. Our proposed methods contribute to more homogeneous data distribution without additional tagging or identification steps. Evaluations through simulations on real-world datasets demonstrate that our proposed methods outstand existing solutions in current learning systems.

A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new regularization technique, combining interpolation methods to enhance semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The proposed strategy uses consistency regularization to ensure the segmentation of mixed data matches the mixed segmentations. This approach belongs to the category of adaptive data regularization techniques that reduce overfitting when working with highly confident labelled data. The method has several advantages over alternative techniques such as adversarial and generative models, primarily due to its minimal computational requirements. Evaluations using publicly available MRI datasets - specifically ACDC and MMWHS - demonstrate that this proposed technique outperforms existing semi-supervised models, with source code available on GitHub.

In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of quantum mechanics' incompleteness, Einstein had already raised these concerns. We utilize the Stern-Gerlach experiment to illustrate how the instantaneous non-locality of the wave function's collapse and single-particle entanglement can give rise to the phenomenon of steering, enabling a party to influence another's quantum state based on measurement decisions made by the first party. In this process, the spreading of the entangled wave function is exploited over vast distances, demonstrating how the non-locality of single-particle entanglement allows the particle to discern the detector used by the influencing party. Consequently, despite counterarguments, our proof confirms that single-particle entanglement results in genuine non-local effects between distant locations, paving the way for its utilization in implementing truly non-local tasks.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and improved information systems within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has yielded substantial benefits, albeit with heightened risks of security breaches and compromised privacy. As IoVs technology continues to evolve, there's growing interest in privacy preservation methodologies that adapt to these changes. Federated Learning has shown promise in safeguarding IoVs data and addressing concerns about security and privacy, whereas Blockchain technology presents possibilities for secure and verifiable data management. This paper conducts an in-depth review of Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning frameworks for IoVs, exploring potential problems, viable solutions, and future directions. This comprehensive survey can serve as a foundation for developing novel BC-Enabled FL solutions to address various IoVs data privacy challenges and scenarios.

Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. In contrast, efficient hardware-friendly alternatives like Gated Recurrent Neural Networks and Graves networks have been showing sub-optimal performance in complex sequence understanding tasks. This study proposes an innovative approach that integrates and optimizes LSTM networks for efficient hardware deployment by applying tensor decompositions and designing customized hardware architectures. By systematically redesigning the hardware architecture to match the properties of tensor-compressed models, a significant performance improvement of 14x is achieved over compressed alternatives while maintaining high accuracy levels comparable to standard LSTM networks. The resulting model GrvTucker demonstrates efficient performance on multiple sequence analysis tasks and can be implemented on low-cost hardware platforms such as FPGAs.

R.W.K. Odoni initially established the connection between the Galois group of an iterated polynomial and the symmetric group in fields of characteristic zero. A generalization to fields of positive characteristic was achieved by Juul. Building on these findings, we explore a scenario involving an irreducible polynomial F over the algebraic closure of a finite field k(t) with algebraic and separable coefficients. When a generic monic polynomial Phi is composed with F, resulting in a new polynomial with coefficients (a0, a1,...), we identify the Galois group of the composite polynomial's mth iterate. The structure of this Galois group mirrors the (m-folded) iterated wreath product of the symmetric group S_(nd) for n > 0, where n represents the polynomial's degree. In the case of large finite fields, the application of this discovery aligns with analogous theories, including the polynomial equivalent of the Bateman-Horn conjecture, the Chowla's conjecture regarding autocorrelation, and the Chebotarev density theorem over function fields.

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly energy-dependent and given specific symmetry conditions, we establish the same optimal blow-up criterion found by Holmer and Roudenko for solutions in an infinite domain. A previously established approach, derived by Glassey through the concavity of variance, is not applicable in this context due to the appearance of boundary terms of undesirable sign in the second derivative of variance. Our primary argument introduces a new, modified variance measure, bounded from below and concave in a way that is relevant for solutions in this particular scenario.

We provide a novel proof that local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric embeddings for a polynomial variety defined over the integers have an equivalent form to local positive-characteristic reductions of the variety for nearly all prime numbers.

Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis, focusing on the underlying statistical concepts and the need for objective utility functions to make informed decisions. We explore various issues with Bayes factor estimates, including their tendency to err and the reliability of bridge sampling, especially when analyzing complex scenarios. To tackle these challenges, we develop a simulation-based approach for validating the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates and examine the stability of Bayes factors in relation to different Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) draws. We also investigate the variability of Bayes factor estimates and the effectiveness of utility functions in making informed decisions. To facilitate the assessment of Bayes factor reliability, we outline a step-by-step workflow that researchers can use to evaluate the performance of Bayes factor analysis for their individual studies, including an illustrative example from the cognitive sciences. We anticipate that this research will contribute to the development of a robust methodology for evaluating scientific hypotheses based on Bayes factor analysis, along with reproducible code available online.

Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to classify sentence pairs as coherent or incoherent based on the presence of discourse indicators, effectively segmenting texts into semantically connected segments. These segmented segments can provide valuable insights into the structure of text, which is crucial for various NLP tasks that analyze the relationships between sentences. In contrast to existing methods that rely on classification tasks between sentence pairs, this research predicts the specific indicators used to segment coherent segments, taking into consideration the semantic context of each pair. Evaluation on a collection of 16 standard datasets demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach in semantically analyzing the structure of texts, achieving F1 scores of 63.2% on a test set of 1000 randomly selected articles from Wikipedia when classifying segmented segments.

Building upon the Jordanian twist concept, we have derived a generalized version. The generalized version, modified in the $r$-symmetrized form, meets the requirements for a 2-cocycle. Notably, the classic Jordanian twist is identified as a specific instance of our generalized version.

This research develops an innovative method for addressing the containment issue with enhanced regular expressions, expanding basic patterns by integrating intersection and complement operators and incorporating regular expressions over infinite domains. Unlike traditional methods limited to finite character sets, our approach accommodates expressions representing sets of strings defined by their durations. We propose an actionable strategy for ascertaining whether one regular expression denotes a subset of another, which may result in expanded regular expressions as evidence of containment. Our findings have practical applications in various fields, including security analysis, protocol verification, and anomaly detection. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we evaluated it using annotated news transcripts and network traffic data showing superior performance compared to existing methods.

Building upon previous work by \cite{Ferrara:1971vh}, \cite{Ferrara:1973vz}, we develop a comprehensive integral representation of conformal block operators in CFT$_2$, specifically tailored for spinning primary fields. Notably, this integral expression can be re-expressed as a product of two weighted AdS$_2$ field combinations when the primary fields in question are conserved, which results in the representation of conserved current conformal block operators in CFT$_2$ in terms of geodesic operators defined within the AdS$_2$ framework rather than the AdS$_3$ framework. Moreover, this new perspective enables a direct mapping between AdS$_2$ and AdS$_3$ geodesic operators through the use of bulk gauge fields. Consequently, this relationship yields a new integral representation of the AdS$_3$ metric that satisfies the equations of motion, which in turn facilitates the expression of conformal block operators in terms of gauge invariant operators constructed from the Weyl tensor rather than the gauge field itself.

To greatly decrease the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a concept called multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics. This configuration involves dividing an LE mirror into multiple sections and using each one to direct X-rays onto a single shared image sensor. If each LE section is arranged in a different rotational position, the system can effectively cover a large area of the sky. A model was created to evaluate the performance of a specific setup with four sectioned mirrors, each with a 15cm radius and 30cm length, rotated by 30 degrees and operated at 10 keV. The results showed that a point source placed directly in front of the LE mirror would produce a strong signal, while sources positioned at the edge of the detectable area would produce a weaker but still measurable response. Notably, the system's ability to distinguish between multiple sources needs further development. However, its potential for large-scale, rapid monitoring of multiple X-ray sources makes it a promising candidate for various applications including on-board satellite systems, ground-based observatories, and laboratory setups.

To investigate the structure of dark matter, a deep learning framework was implemented to explore the impact of cosmic velocity fields on halo formation. In this cosmological simulation, dark matter particles were represented by a set of features including mass, velocity, and positional data. A graph neural network was trained to identify halos, and in a set of five independent runs of a massive simulation, cosmic velocity fields were incorporated to assess their impact on halo detection. Results showed that without the velocity field, the network failed to recognize several halo characteristics, but including this parameter improved the construction of dark matter structures. Notably, a Delta$V_{\rm MPT}$ smoothing method revealed the influence of local velocity fields on halo formation, contrasting with a globally smoothed effect of the velocity field. These findings highlight the importance of cosmic velocity field information in halo identification and suggest its potential use in future large-scale simulations and models of dark matter.

One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect these minuscule magnetic fields. As a superconductor's expelled field generates a gradient near its surface, it induces a centripetal force that affects atomic motion within the interferometer, making it possible to measure this effect through atomic interference patterns. Based on the $10^{-12}$ g accuracy achieved in atomic gravity measurements, it's theoretically possible to measure expelled local magnetic field strengths at levels as precise as $10^{-14}$ Tesla.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. In the case of the isolated Mn adatom, slight spin-orbit coupling effects were observed, while localized spin polarization on Nb atoms showed marginal influence. Additionally, by scaling the exchange field, the absence of a $d_{x^2-y^2}$-like YSR state in the spectrum was explained. For a close-packed ferromagnetic dimer, satisfactory agreement with experimental results regarding YSR state splitting was found. However, for an antiferromagnetic dimer, spin-orbit coupling was insufficient to account for observed state splitting. Reversal of the magnetic dimer's moment alignment led to YSR state splitting, along with a notable shift in energy and formation of a zero-bias peak for the most deeply seated YSR state.

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focusing on skin cancer detection using a dataset of 2,480 images. Our primary contribution involves using a dataset with balanced classes to train a classifier, which is then applied to the challenge dataset to prioritize uncertain images for a data annotator's review. The ultimate classification is determined by the most frequent output of the annotator. Additionally, we proposed an ensemble method combining multiple deep learning models, which resulted in significant accuracy improvements.

Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to radiate forward and resemble weak boson colliders beyond a few TeV, a new perspective is taken that treats weak bosons as fundamental components of these leptons. Within this context of a muon collider, we evaluate the relevance of W and Z particle distribution functions, particularly at their leading order, during both symmetric and asymmetric energy collisions. A comparison is made between EM-only and EW-inclusive simulations to determine the impact of vacuum polarization effects. A survey of current and projected data from various leptonic and hadronic processes at different energy levels in both identical and non-identical multi-lepton final states is also performed. In the case of non-linear EW field effects, a significant improvement is necessary for more precise simulations, ideally through a EW-inclusive framework like EWMC@NLO or RES-BHPS, especially when exploring final states close to the threshold for muon triangle production.

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of key terminology and discuss specific conditions required for fixed points to be considered stable or unstable. We analyze the state of research on clustering properties of fractional order dynamical systems and explore the connection between invariant manifolds and their clustering properties. Using our established definitions, we demonstrate how specific external forces result in a clustering property, and under conditions similar to those found in previous studies, we prove that certain fractional order dynamical systems without disturbances exhibit a desired stability property. Additionally, we provide an example to show that the term stable is insufficient without specific conditions for a positive result on the desired clustering properties in fractional order dynamical systems.

This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate.

Within the simplest scoto-seesaw model, we examine the consistency between the electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino characteristics, and dark matter behavior. By integrating the minimal dark sector into the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw framework, we establish a comprehensive understanding of neutrino oscillation lengths. Here, the "atmospheric" mass scale is directly produced at tree level, whereas the "solar" scale arises through radiative processes, mediated by the dark sector. Furthermore, we determine the parameter ranges that meet theoretical requirements, in addition to dark matter relic abundance and direct detection standards. Utilizing two-loop renormalization group equations, we assess the stability of the vacuum and verify the consistency of the inherent dark parity symmetry. Consequently, we derive a minimum threshold for the neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude.
